questions.question: Patient following RTA was brought to ED, where he was told that his ulnar nerve is injured. Which of the following muscles would be affected in this patient?

explanation.text: Image shows the thenar muscles of the hand.

**Only thenar muscle of the hand supplied by the ulnar nerve is Adductor pollicis (Option A):** which would be affected in this scenario. Rest of the muscles of thenar eminence are supplied by the median nerve. Muscles of Thenar Eminence: Muscle Attachments Nerve supply Action Abductor pollicis brevis (Option C) Origin: Scaphoid tubercle, crest of Trapezium and flexor retinaculum Insertion: Base of proximal phalanx of thumb Median nerve Abduction of thumb Flexor pollicis brevis (Option B)

Origin: Capitate, crest of Trapezium and flexor retinaculum Insertion: Base of proximal phalanx of thumb Median nerve Flexion of metacarpo-phalangeal joint of thumb Opponens pollicis (Option D) Origin: crest of Trapezium and flexor retinaculum Insertion: Lateral half of palmar surface of the shaft of thumb metacarpal Median nerve Opposition of thumb towards fingers Adductor pollicis (Option A) Origin: Oblique head- base of 2nd-3rd metacarpal; transverse head- shaft of 3rd metacarpal Insertion: Base of proximal phalanx of thumb (medial aspect) Ulnar nerve Adduction of thumb Clinical Tests: Abductor pollicis brevis: Pen test is done.

Patient is asked to abduct the thumb. Patients will be unable to do so in case of median nerve injury Adductor pollicis: Froment's sign, also known as the book test, evaluates the function of the adductor pollicis muscle (supplied by ulnar nerve).

When a patient is asked to firmly grip a book between the thumbs and fingers of both hands, the thumb on the affected side flexes at the interphalangeal joint (flexor pollicis longus, innervated by the median nerve).

questions.question: In which sequence do the following carpal bones typically ossify: capitate, pisiform, scaphoid?

explanation.text: Carpal bones are 8 short bones arranged in 2 rows, each with 4 bones in the region of the wrist. From lateral to medial, bones of the proximal row are the scaphoid, lunate, triquetral, and pisiform, and those of the distal row are the trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, and hamate.

Carpal Bones Ossification Age Capitate (First one to ossify) 1-3 Months Hamate 2-4 Months Triquetrum During 3rd year of life Lunate During 4th year of life Scaphoid During 5th year of life Trapezium During 6th year of life Trapezoid During 6-7th year of life Pisiform (Last one to ossify) During 9-12th year of life

questions.question: Which of the following muscles is responsible for flexing the distal interphalangeal joints of the fingers?

explanation.text: The flexor digitorum profundus (FDP) is responsible for flexing the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints of the 2nd to 5th fingers. The muscles of the anterior compartment of forearm are the flexor-pronator muscles and arranged in 3 layers: Superficial layer: Pronator teres Flexor carpi radialis Flexor carpi ulnaris Palmaris longus Intermediate layer: Flexor digitorum superficialis Deep layer: 1.

Flexor digitorum profundus: Origin Proximal three-quarters of the anterior and medial surfaces of the ulna and the interosseous membrane. Insertion Bases of the distal phalanges of the 2nd to 5th digits. Action Flexes the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints of the 2nd to 5th fingers and flexion of wrist. Nerve Supply Medial part by ulnar nerve and lateral part by median nerve (C8, T1) 2.

Flexor Pollicis Longus: Origin Anterior surface of the radius and adjacent interosseous membrane. Insertion Base of the distal phalanx of the thumb. Action Flexion of phalanges of thumb Nerve Supply Median nerve (anterior interosseous branch) (C8, T1). 3. Pronator Quadratus: Origin Distal one-quarter of the anterior surface of the ulna. Insertion Distal one-quarter of the anterior surface of the radius.
Action Pronation of the forearm (pulls the radius over the ulna). Nerve Supply Median nerve (anterior interosseous branch) (C8, T1).

questions.question: A 35-year-old carpenter presents with pain and weakness in his right forearm after repetitive hammering. On examination, you note tenderness over the medial epicondyle and weakness in wrist flexion. There is no sensory loss. Based on these findings, which muscle is not likely involved?

explanation.text: Flexor pollicis longus is a deep muscle of the anterior compartment of forearm which helps in flexion of distal phalanges of the thumb and no action in flexion of wrist. The muscles of the anterior compartment of forearm are the flexor-pronator muscles and arranged in 3 layers: Superficial layer: Pronator teres Flexor carpi

radialis Flexor carpi ulnaris Palmaris longus Intermediate layer: Flexor digitorum superficialis Deep layer: Flexor digitorum profundus Flexor pollicis longus Pronator quadratus Superficial muscles of anterior compartment of forearm consists of 5 muscles: 1.

Pronator teres: Origin Humeral head- Medial epicondyle of the humerus (via the common flexor tendon) Ulnar head - Coronoid process of the ulna Insertion Lateral surface of the midshaft of the radius. Action Pronates the forearm and weak flexor of elbow. Nerve Supply Median nerve (C6, C7). 2. Flexor Carpi Radialis (FCR): Origin Medial epicondyle of the humerus (via the common flexor tendon). Insertion Base of the second and third metacarpal bones.

Action Flexes and abducts the wrist (radial deviation). Nerve Supply Median nerve (C6, C7). 3. Palmaris Longus: Origin Medial epicondyle of the humerus (via the common flexor tendon). Insertion Flexor retinaculum and palmar aponeurosis. Action Flexion of hand at wrist makes palmar aponeurosis tense. Nerve Supply Median nerve (C7, C8). 4.

Flexor Carpi Ulnaris: Origin Humeral head- Medial epicondyle of the humerus (via the common flexor tendon) Ulnar head- Olecranon and posterior border of the ulna. Insertion Pisiform, hook of hamate, and base of the fifth metacarpal. Action Flexes and adducts the wrist Nerve Supply Ulnar nerve (C7, C8). 5.

Flexor Digitorum Superficialis: Origin Humeroulnar head- Medial epicondyle of the humerus and coronoid process of the ulna Radial head- Oblique line of the radius Insertion Middle phalanges of the 2nd to 5th digits. Action Flexion of middle and proximal phalanges of digits. Nerve Supply Median nerve (C7, C8, T1)

questions.question: A surgeon is performing an axillary dissection for breast cancer and must be cautious not to damage structures piercing the clavipectoral fascia. Which of the following statements about these structures is TRUE?

options.A: The cephalic vein pierces the clavipectoral fascia and runs through the deltopectoral groove before draining into the axillary vein.
options.B: The thoracoacromial artery pierces the clavipectoral fascia and divides into pectoral, deltoid, axillary, and clavicular branches.
options.C: Lateral pectoral nerve passes through the clavipectoral fascia and innervates the pectoralis minor muscle after piercing the pectoralis major.
options.D: Lymphatic vessels draining the lateral breast region pierce the clavipectoral fascia and drain into the central axillary lymph nodes.

explanation.text: The cephalic vein courses in the deltopectoral groove, then pierces the clavipectoral fascia to drain into the axillary vein. It is a reliable landmark during axillary dissections and must be preserved or ligated with care.

Clavipectoral Fascia and Piercing Structures: Feature Description Location Lies deep to pectoralis major, extends from clavicle to axillary fascia Pierced by Cephalic vein Thoracoacromial artery and its branches Lateral pectoral nerve Lymphatics from lateral breast Clinical relevance During axillary dissection, these structures must be protected Feature Details Cephalic vein (Option A) Arises from dorsal venous network of the hand Runs in deltopectoral groove with deltoid branch of thoracoacromial artery Pierces clavipectoral fascia to drain into axillary vein Thoracoacromial artery (Option B) Branch of second part of axillary artery Pierces clavipectoral fascia Gives off pectoral, deltoid, clavicular, acromial branches (no 'axillary' branch) Lateral pectoral nerve (Option C) Arises from lateral cord of brachial plexus Pierces clavipectoral fascia near thoracoacromial artery Passes medial to pectoralis minor Innervates pectoralis major only Lymphatics (Option D) Drain lateral breast and pectoral region Pierce clavipectoral fascia to reach apical axillary lymph nodes, not central nodes Suspensory ligament of axilla Inferior extension of clavipectoral fascia Anchors axillary fascia to maintain axillary fossa concavity

questions.question: Which of the following statements is TRUE regarding the rotator cuff muscles?

options.A: The rotator cuff includes the Supraspinatus, Infraspinatus, Subscapularis, and Teres major, which collectively aid in shoulder abduction and external rotation.
options.B: The Subscapularis is the only rotator cuff muscle involved in internal rotation of the humerus.
options.C: The Infraspinatus and Teres minor are responsible for medial rotation of the shoulder joint.
options.D: The rotator cuff muscles are primarily located in the anterior aspect of the shoulder joint

explanation.text: Rotator Cuff Muscles: Muscle (Tendon) Action Nerve Supply Supraspinatus Initiates abduction of the shoulder Suprascapular nerve(C5,C6) Infraspinatus External(lateral)rotation of the shoulder Suprascapular nerve(C5,C6) Teres minor External(lateral) rotation of the shoulder Axillary nerve (C5,C6) Subscapularis Internal (medial) rotation of the shoulder Upper and lower subscapular nerves (C5,C6,C7) The rotator cuff is composed of the Supraspinatus, Infraspinatus, Subscapularis, and Teres minor, not Teres major (Option A).

The Infraspinatus and Teres minor are involved in external (lateral) rotation, not medial rotation. (Option C) The rotator cuff muscles are located primarily around the shoulder joint, with some being posterior (e.g., Infraspinatus, Teres minor) and one anterior (Subscapularis) (Option D).

questions.question: Which of the following fasciae is the axillary sheath derived from?

explanation.text: The axillary sheath is derived from the prevertebral layer of deep cervical fascia.

Apex/Cervicoaxillary Canal: Directed upwards and medially towards the root of the neck Axillary artery, axillary vein, and brachial plexus enter the axilla through this canal Axillary vessels and cords of the brachial plexus are in the axillary sheath which is derived from the prevertebral layer of deep cervical fascia Boundaries of Cervicoaxillary Canal: Anteriorly Posterior surface of the clavicle Posteriorly Superior border of the scapula and medial aspect of the coracoid process Medially Outer border of the first rib Contents of the Axilla: Axillary artery and its branches Axillary vein and its tributaries Infraclavicular part of the brachial plexus Five groups of axillary lymph nodes and the associated lymphatics The long thoracic and intercostobrachial nerves Axillary fat and areolar tissue in which the other contents are embedded

questions.question: A 35-year-old construction worker falls from a ladder and lands on his outstretched hand, resulting in a clavicular fracture as shown in the X- Ray given below. Which ligament plays a crucial role in stabilizing the medial end of the clavicle to the first rib, preventing excessive elevation of the clavicle?

explanation.text: Costoclavicular ligament anchors the medial end of the clavicle to the first rib and acts as a strong stabilizer that limits excessive elevation of the clavicle. It is critical in maintaining clavicular positioning, particularly during weight-bearing activities involving the upper limb. The clavicle is often fractured by an indirect fall on an outstretched hand.

The most common fracture site is at the junction of its two curvatures, the weakest point. The lateral fragment is displaced downward due to the weight of the limb, as the trapezius muscle cannot fully support it.

Location on Clavicle Attachment Lateral End (Acromial end) Joint capsule of the acromioclavicular joint Medial End (Sternal end) Fibrous capsule of sternoclavicular joint (all around) Articular disc (posterosuperiorly) Interclavicular ligament (superiorly) Lateral One-Third of Shaft Anterior border: Origin of deltoid muscle Posterior border: Insertion of trapezius muscle Conoid tubercle and trapezoid ridge: Attachment to the conoid and trapezoid parts of coracoclavicular ligament Medial Two-Thirds of Shaft Anterior surface: Origin of pectoralis major Rough superior surface: Origin of clavicular head of sternocleidomastoid Oval impression (inferior surface, medial end): Attachment of costoclavicular ligament Subclavian groove: Insertion of subclavius muscle, margins give attachment to clavipectoral fascia Posterior surface (near medial end): Origin of sternohyoid muscle Coracoclavicular ligament (Option A) primarily stabilizes the lateral end of the clavicle by connecting it to the coracoid process of the scapula, providing support for the acromioclavicular joint.
Weight transmission from upper limb to axial skeleton.
**Sternoclavicular ligament (Option C):** While this ligament supports the sternoclavicular joint and maintains joint integrity, it is not the primary structure responsible for
limiting clavicular elevation. The costoclavicular ligament plays a more crucial role in this function.

**Interclavicular ligament (Option D):** connects the medial ends of the clavicles and provides stability across the jugular notch of the sternum. Its primary function is to prevent excessive depression of the clavicle, not elevation.

questions.question: A 45-year-old painter presents with shoulder pain and weakness, particularly when raising his arm. He reports difficulty lifting objects overhead. On physical examination, there is tenderness over the shoulder and weakness in initiating arm abduction. Which rotator cuff muscle is most likely injured?

explanation.text: Supraspinatus is responsible for initiating arm abduction, commonly injured in overhead activities like painting.

Rotator Cuff Muscles Muscles and muscle action The rotator cuff consists of four muscles: Supraspinatus: Located above the scapular spine, it aids in arm abduction and is the most commonly injured rotator cuff muscle. (Option C) Infraspinatus: Below the scapular spine, it helps with lateral arm rotation and shoulder stabilization. (Option A ruled out) Teres Minor: Works with the infraspinatus in lateral rotation and stabilizing the shoulder. (Option B ruled out) Subscapularis: On the front of the scapula, it is responsible for medial arm rotation and is the only rotator cuff muscle that doesn’t attach to the greater tubercle of the humerus and forgotten tendon. (Option D ruled out) Musculotendinous Cuff: The tendons of these muscles form the rotator cuff, which supports and stabilizes the shoulder joint during movement.

Functions Stabilize the shoulder. Rotate the arm (medially and laterally). Assist with arm abduction. Control arm movement, especially overhead. Clinical Relevance Rotator cuff tears: Resulting in pain, weakness, and limited movement. Subacromial bursitis: Inflammation causing shoulder pain and stiffness. Axillary nerve injury: Can weaken shoulder abduction by affecting the deltoid muscle.

Muscle (Tendon) Action Nerve supply Supraspinatus Initiates abduction of the shoulder Suprascapular nerve(C5,C6) Infraspinatus External and lateral rotation of the shoulder Suprascapular nerve(C5,C6) Teres minor External and lateral rotation of the shoulder Axillary nerve (C5,C6) Subscapularis Internal and medial rotation of the shoulder Upper and lower subscapular nerves (C5,C6,C7)

questions.question: A 60-year-old female patient presents to the ED with a tension pneumothorax. The physician decides to perform a chest drain insertion to relieve the pressure. As the physician prepares for the procedure, they review the anatomical landmarks to ensure they insert the drain safely. Which muscle defines the posterior boundary of the Triangle of Safety, ensuring that the physician avoids vital structures during the chest drain insertion?

explanation.text: The lateral border of the latissimus dorsi muscle forms the posterior boundary of the Triangle of Safety for ICD insertion. Triangle of Safety for Intercostal Chest Drain (ICD) insertion: Anatomical area on the lateral chest wall where it is considered safest to insert a chest drain. Boundaries of the triangle: Anteriorly Lateral border of the pectoralis major muscle. Posteriorly Lateral border of the latissimus dorsi muscle.

Inferiorly A horizontal line at the level of the 5th intercostal space (usually aligned with the nipple in males). Superiorly Base of the axilla(armpit). This area minimizes the risk of injury to vital structures such as nerves, blood vessels, and the lung itself. The drain is typically inserted in the 4th or 5th intercostal space along the mid-axillary line.

questions.question: Which muscle forms the medial border of the Triangle of Auscultation?

explanation.text: The medial border of the Triangle of Auscultation is formed by the lateral edge of the trapezius muscle. Triangle of Auscultation: Anatomical Location: Located on the posterior thorax, specifically on the back,

just below the scapula. Boundaries: Medial Border Lateral border of the trapezius muscle. Lateral Border Medial border of the scapula. Inferior Border Superior border of the latissimus dorsi muscle. Anterior or floor Rhomboid major, 6th and 7th ribs. Clinical Significance: This area is important for auscultating lung sounds because it is relatively free from muscle and bone interference.

It allows for clearer sounds of breath, particularly in patients with respiratory issues. Positioning: To enhance the visibility and accessibility of the triangle, patients are often instructed to lean forward and cross their arms, which brings the scapulae apart and exposes this area.

questions.question: Which of the following nerves is responsible for winging of scapula?

explanation.text: Winging of the scapula occurs due to paralysis or weakness of the serratus anterior muscle, which is innervated by the long thoracic nerve. The serratus anterior muscle normally holds the scapula against the thoracic wall. Damage to the long thoracic nerve results in a characteristic “winged” appearance of the scapula, especially when the patient pushes against a wall.
**Dorsal scapular nerve (Option A):** Innervates the rhomboid major and minor and levator scapulae, which retract and elevate the scapula. Injury to this nerve does not cause winging of the scapula.

**Spinal accessory nerve (Option B):** Innervates the trapezius muscle, which elevates and rotates the scapula. Damage leads to shoulder drooping and difficulty elevating the arm but does not cause scapular winging.

**Suprascapular nerve (Option D):** Innervates the supraspinatus and infraspinatus muscles, which assist in shoulder abduction and external rotation. Injury affects shoulder movement, not scapular positioning.

questions.question: A patient with a humeral fracture presents with difficulty extending the elbow and wrist. Which of the following nerves is most likely affected?

explanation.text: Radial nerve innervates the extensor muscles of the upper limb, including the triceps brachii (for elbow extension) and the extensor muscles of the forearm (for wrist extension). It passes through the spiral groove of the humerus and is therefore at risk in humeral shaft fractures. Damage to the radial nerve leads to wrist drop (inability to extend the wrist) and loss of elbow extension.

**Nerves Related to Humerus Nerve Location Relative to Humerus Axillary Nerve (Option D):** Around the surgical neck of the humerus. Musculocutaneous Nerve It originates from the lateral cord of the brachial plexus, pierces coracobrachialis, travels between biceps and coracobrachialis.
**Radial Nerve (Option A):** Passes through the spiral groove of the humerus, posterior to the brachial artery, anterior to the long head of triceps.
**Median Nerve (Option B):** Passes anterior to the humerus, but does not innervate upper arm muscles.
**Ulnar Nerve (Option C):** Travels down the medial side of the brachium, behind the medial epicondyle of the humerus.
